management-system.definition: The set of policies, processes, roles and records an organisation uses to set objectives and achieve them.

harmonised-structure.definition: The common clause structure (4 to 10) shared by all ISO management system standards, so one system can serve several standards.

context-of-the-organisation.definition: The internal and external issues that affect the organisation's ability to achieve the intended results of its management system.

interested-party.definition: A person or organisation that can affect, be affected by, or believe itself affected by a decision or activity, such as customers, employees or regulators.

scope.definition: The boundaries of the management system: which sites, activities, products and services it covers.

top-management.definition: The person or group who directs and controls the organisation at the highest level and is accountable for the management system.

policy.definition: The intentions and direction of an organisation, formally expressed by its top management.

objective.definition: A result to be achieved. Objectives should be measurable, monitored, communicated and updated.

risk.definition: The effect of uncertainty on objectives, often described by the likelihood of an event and its consequences.

opportunity.definition: A situation that can lead to a positive result, such as a new market, a better technology or a more efficient way of working.

risk-assessment.definition: The overall process of identifying, analysing and evaluating risks.

risk-treatment.definition: The process of modifying a risk: avoiding it, reducing it with controls, sharing it, or accepting it.

residual-risk.definition: The risk that remains after treatment. The risk owner must accept it.

risk-owner.definition: The person with the accountability and authority to manage a risk.

control.definition: A measure that maintains or modifies risk, such as a procedure, a technical safeguard or a physical barrier.

statement-of-applicability.definition: The document listing the ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A controls, whether each is applied, and the justification for including or excluding it.

competence.definition: The ability to apply knowledge and skills to achieve intended results.

awareness.definition: People knowing the policy, their contribution to the management system and the consequences of not following it.

ai-literacy.definition: The skills, knowledge and understanding people need to use AI systems in an informed way and to be aware of their opportunities, risks and possible harm.

documented-information.definition: Information an organisation must control and maintain, and the medium it is on: documents that describe how to work and records that show what was done.

procedure.definition: A specified way to carry out an activity or a process.

record.definition: Documented information that states results achieved or provides evidence of activities performed. Records are not changed after the fact.

process.definition: A set of related activities that uses inputs to deliver an intended result.

process-approach.definition: Managing activities as connected processes, with clear inputs, outputs, owners and measures, rather than as separate departments.

pdca.definition: The improvement cycle behind every management system: plan, carry out, check the results, and act on what you learn.

monitoring.definition: Determining the status of a system, process or activity, often by checking or observing it over time.

kpi.definition: A measurable value that shows how well a process or objective is performing.

internal-audit.definition: A systematic, independent check, carried out by or for the organisation, of whether the management system meets its requirements and works effectively.

audit-criteria.definition: The requirements an audit compares the evidence against, such as a standard, a policy or a contract.

audit-finding.definition: The result of comparing audit evidence with the audit criteria: a conformity, a nonconformity or an opportunity for improvement.

management-review.definition: A planned review by top management of whether the management system is still suitable, adequate and effective.

nonconformity.definition: The non-fulfilment of a requirement, whether from a standard, the law, a customer or your own procedures.

major-nonconformity.definition: A nonconformity that means a requirement is not met at all, or that the system cannot achieve its intended results. It can block certification.

correction.definition: Action to fix a detected nonconformity, such as reworking a product. It does not remove the cause.

corrective-action.definition: Action to remove the cause of a nonconformity and prevent it from happening again.

root-cause.definition: The underlying reason a problem occurred. Removing it prevents the problem from coming back.

continual-improvement.definition: Recurring activity to enhance performance, for example through corrective actions, audits and reviews.

effectiveness.definition: The extent to which planned activities are carried out and planned results are achieved.

outsourced-process.definition: A process an external organisation performs for you. You remain responsible for it and must control it.

information-security.definition: Preserving the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information.

cia-triad.definition: Confidentiality: only authorised people can read the information. Integrity: it is accurate and complete. Availability: it can be used when needed.

information-security-incident.definition: One or more unwanted security events that are likely to harm the organisation's information or operations.

asset.definition: Anything of value to the organisation, such as information, software, equipment, services or people's knowledge.

personal-data.definition: Any information about an identified or identifiable living person, such as a name, an email address or an employee number.

controller.definition: The organisation that decides why and how personal data is processed.

processor.definition: An organisation that processes personal data on behalf of a controller, under a data processing agreement.

lawful-basis.definition: One of the six legal grounds that allow personal data to be processed, such as consent, a contract or a legal obligation.

ropa.definition: The register of how and why an organisation processes personal data, required by the GDPR.

dpia.definition: An assessment of the risks to people's rights before starting processing that is likely to result in a high risk.

personal-data-breach.definition: A security breach that leads to personal data being lost, destroyed, changed or disclosed without authorisation. It must usually be reported to the authority within 72 hours.

ai-system.definition: A machine-based system that infers from its input how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions.

high-risk-ai-system.definition: An AI system the EU AI Act classifies as high-risk, for example in recruitment or critical infrastructure. It must meet strict requirements before use.

deployer.definition: An organisation that uses an AI system under its authority in a professional activity.

human-oversight.definition: Measures that let people understand, monitor and, when needed, override or stop an AI system.

compliance-obligation.definition: A legal requirement, or another requirement the organisation has chosen to follow, such as a customer contract or an industry code.

environmental-aspect.definition: An element of the organisation's activities, products or services that interacts with the environment, such as energy use or waste.

hazard.definition: A source with the potential to cause injury or ill health.

near-miss.definition: An event where no one was hurt and nothing was damaged, but could have been. Reporting near misses helps prevent real incidents.

certification-audit.definition: An audit by an independent certification body that decides whether the organisation's management system can be certified against a standard.
